title: Common Core W.CCR.7 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. unpacks the seventh Common Core writing anchor standard, which calls for short and sustained research projects built on focused questions. Rather than restating the standard, he isolates three features he considers distinctive: varied project lengths, focused research questions, and a demonstration of newfound understanding. He argues that shorter projects give students more repetitions in the core research skills of framing a question, choosing a strategy, judging sources and integrating findings. Drawing on his own failures with open-ended topic assignments, he contends that research becomes boring and shapeless without a sharply focused question. He then models the move from broad topics to focused prompts and offers unit-linked research questions from his own English classes. The piece closes with reflection questions students can use to articulate what their research taught them.
points: Stuart plans one extended research project per year and at least one short project per unit so that research skills can be explicitly taught and assessed in focused repetitions.

His confessed failure with open-ended topic research produced a stack of papers merely 'about' global warming or abortion, which he uses to argue that student choice without a focused question yields shallow work.
He models converting broad topics into focused, arguable prompts and ties research questions directly to novels in his curriculum, such as All Quiet on the Western Front and Things Fall Apart.

Students should demonstrate what they learned in forms ranging from a single paragraph to a sustained paper, in narrative (I-search), explanatory or argumentative modes, followed by reflection on challenges faced.
quotes: This standard is part of a trio of “Research to Build and Present Knowledge” anchor standards (W.CCR.7-9). Since the three are somewhat overlapping, I'm going to focus on the three aspects of W.CCR.7 that make it unique.

My goal next year is for at least one extended research project during the entire year and at least one short research project per unit. This will allow me to explicitly teach and assess the skills listed above in a focused manner.

For example, I've been the knucklehead who assigns an open-ended research project with way too little guidance. I thought I was awesome — kids were going to get to research something that they were genuinely interested in.

Research and explain three of the African continent's greatest strengths and three of its greatest weaknesses. Based on your findings, what are key ways that people outside of Africa can help the continent to continue growing and recovering from centuries of ill-use?

Finally, students need to demonstrate what they've learned in their research — this could be done in a single-paragraph or as a more sustained paper. It could be done in a meta fashion (e.g., an I-search narrative), an explanatory fashion, or an argumentative fashion.
